description: A team of passionate innovators exploring the intersection of AI, technology, and creativity to solve real-world problems. We turn ideas into impactful solutions through collaboration, experimentation, and continuous learning.
summary:
FireHarmonics goes beyond collecting data for display. We combine web tools and AI-assisted development to analyse satellite observations. Our work centres on one question: Did fire activity change, or did the satellite observing it change?

Our focus is satellite sensor compatibility. FireHarmonics harmonises NASA FIRMS observations from MODIS and VIIRS into a fire-activity calendar from 2002 onward. We account for spatial resolution and daytime/nighttime detection differences, while NOAA-20 observations, calibrated through S-NPP to the Aqua MODIS reference, extend the record as older satellites retire.

We calibrated on 2012–2016 data and reconstructed MODIS observations for 2017–2021 using VIIRS alone. Median annual errors were 12–18%, compared with 459–508% for uncalibrated VIIRS.

Users select any location on Earth through an interactive 3D globe and generate reports showing seasonal patterns, anomalies and uncertainty, subject to data availability. Satellite detections do not equate to individual fires. Cached archives reduce waiting time.

Accessibility features include keyboard navigation, high-contrast views, colour-blind-friendly palettes and reduced motion. We display an experimental ML forecast alongside a seasonal baseline, with the ML forecast labelled as unvalidated.

Our aim is to help people understand how burning activity has changed over time, without mistaking changes in satellite detection for changes on Earth.
details:
OUR IDEA AND PURPOSE

FireHarmonics’ main functionality consists of not only collecting data for display, but also analysing it. Furthermore, our project tackles the problem of harmonising data from different satellite sensors for subsequent analysis. Our work centres on one question: Did fire activity change, or did the satellite observing it change?

MODIS and VIIRS provide valuable records of burning activity, but differences between their observations make direct comparison difficult. A rise in detected hotspots can reflect a more sensitive sensor rather than an actual increase in burning. With that in mind, our main goal was to harmonise these records into a shared fire-activity calendar from 2002 onward.

We chose this challenge specifically because we found the combination of modern technology and Earth science fascinating. It gave us an opportunity to apply our technical skills to a practical problem by making historical satellite observations easier to compare and interpret.

HOW WE HARMONISE THE DATA

Our central focus is compatibility between satellite sensors. We connect Aqua MODIS, S-NPP VIIRS and NOAA-20 VIIRS through a calibration chain, using periods of overlapping observations to estimate how their measurements relate to each other.

Aqua MODIS provides the reference scale. S-NPP VIIRS observations are calibrated to that scale, while NOAA-20 observations are calibrated through S-NPP. This allows newer satellite observations to extend the record as older satellites stop providing data.

Before calibration, we aggregate detections into approximately 1 km active grid cells for daytime or nighttime overpasses. This reduces differences caused when VIIRS records several smaller pixels within the same grid cell. These cells represent observed activity; they do not represent individual fires or the total area burned. A persistent fire may also be detected during multiple overpasses.

We apply separate daytime and nighttime calibration coefficients because detection differences vary between day and night. Where local observations are limited, regional partial pooling allows the estimate to draw on both local observations and a broader regional estimate.

The resulting calendar includes monthly 90% uncertainty intervals, calculated using bootstrap resampling across years combined with counting-noise estimates. Missing observations remain missing instead of being interpreted as zero activity. The harmonisation method is experimental, and its limitations are displayed alongside the results.

HOW WE TEST THE METHOD

We test the harmonisation by asking whether VIIRS can reconstruct MODIS observations that were not used during calibration.

In our “MODIS-Off Test,” coefficients are fitted using observations from 2012–2016. We then use VIIRS alone to reconstruct MODIS activity for 2017–2021 and compare the results with the withheld MODIS observations. This evaluates performance beyond the period used to fit the coefficients.

Our preliminary evaluations reported median annual reconstruction errors of 12–18%, compared with 459–508% for uncalibrated VIIRS. These figures measure reconstruction of the MODIS reference, rather than accuracy in counting individual fires. They apply to the evaluated locations and configurations and do not guarantee the same performance everywhere.

A corresponding test evaluates the NOAA-20-to-S-NPP bridge. Reports include location-specific validation where sufficient observations are available, so users can examine how well the method performs for their selected area.

FROM HISTORICAL ARCHIVES TO AN ACCESSIBLE REPORT

Users select a location through search, geographic coordinates or an interactive 3D globe. They can choose an analysis radius of 10, 25, 50 or 100 km around the selected point. Selecting a country on the globe helps users navigate; the analysis covers the chosen circular area.

Completed years are retrieved from cached annual archives, reducing processing time by avoiding repeated API requests and parsing of historical data. Recent observations may still require requests through the NASA FIRMS API.

After the area is selected and the analysis is completed, FireHarmonics generates a report showing the harmonised calendar, seasonal patterns, anomalies, trends and uncertainty. Users can explore historically active periods, compare activity across years and export results as PDF, JSON or CSV.

For example, a user investigating an unusually active month can compare it with the same calendar month in previous years, examine the uncertainty interval and review the local validation results. These elements help the user judge how strongly the available observations support the apparent change.

ORIGINAL DESIGN AND ACCESSIBILITY

Our team created the original UI and UX design in Figma and implemented it in the web application. The interface brings area selection, the fire-activity calendar and supporting analysis into a shared workflow.

Accessibility features include keyboard navigation, high-contrast views, colour-blind-friendly palettes and reduced-motion options. These features allow users to explore the information through different display and interaction preferences.

Data coverage, uncertainty and methodological limitations are presented alongside the findings so users can consider them when interpreting the report.

EXPERIMENTAL FORECASTING

Alongside historical analysis, FireHarmonics includes an experimental XGBoost model and a seasonal baseline based on historical patterns. These are two forecasting approaches to the same target: the probability of at least one qualifying S-NPP VIIRS vegetation-fire detection within the selected area during the target month.

This target uses the S-NPP VIIRS observation record and is separate from the harmonised calendar. It describes the likelihood of a qualifying satellite detection, rather than the likelihood of a new wildfire starting.

In the current implementation, XGBoost did not demonstrate the improvement over the seasonal baseline required for selection. The baseline therefore provides the selected forecast, while XGBoost results are displayed for comparison and clearly labelled “Experimental · Not validated · May be inaccurate.”

TECHNOLOGY AND ENGINEERING

We combined modern web technologies and AI-assisted development to build the application. The backend uses Python, FastAPI, pandas and NumPy, with PyArrow and Parquet for efficient historical-data storage. The frontend uses React and TypeScript, Three.js for the interactive globe and Recharts for visualisations.

NASA FIRMS supplies the satellite observations, while Natural Earth supplies geographic boundaries. The application is deployed on Microsoft Azure using Caddy and Cloudflare. Our testing tools include pytest, Vitest, Playwright and axe.

We also addressed a broken object-level authorisation issue affecting analysis jobs. Token-based access controls restrict cancellation and restart actions to the user who initiated the analysis.

Claude Code and Codex assisted software development, while ChatGPT assisted with refining the submission text.

INTENDED IMPACT

FireHarmonics is intended to help fire managers, scientists and land managers recognise unusual burning activity and identify historically active periods, providing context for monitoring and planning.

Our contribution is a harmonised calendar that users can explore together with its uncertainty, validation results and limitations. By including validation within each report, we make the evidence behind the comparison accessible to the people using it.

Our aim is to make long-term burning activity easier to understand as satellite technology changes, while giving users the information they need to judge how much confidence to place in the patterns they see.
